think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 21-year-old man from rural Morocco with canine contact presents with an insidious 12-year history of mild right upper quadrant discomfort that acutely worsened with nausea and vomiting. Imaging reveals extensive multilocular and unilocular cystic lesions throughout the right hepatic lobe and disseminated across multiple peritoneal spaces including the iliac fossae. The clinical dilemma is distinguishing multifocal hydatid cyst dissemination—often caused by silent spontaneous rupture or microperforation—from non-parasitic congenital polycystic liver/peritoneal disease or cystic peritoneal carcinomatosis, especially given normal liver enzymes and absence of peripheral eosinophilia.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint is established following clinical evaluation, normal routine laboratory investigations (CBC, transaminases, plain chest radiography), and abdominal ultrasound/CT imaging showing hepatic and peritoneal cysts, prior to specialized hydatid serology (IHA, Novalisa ELISA), prolonged antiparasitic medical therapy, and exploratory laparotomy with parasitological examination.
3. Differential Distinctions: Congenital polycystic liver disease and simple mesenteric/peritoneal cysts were considered given the multicystic hepatic and peritoneal distribution in a young adult, but were distinguished by specific cyst internal architecture (multilocular with daughter vesicles, Gharbi type IV, CE1-CE3a), markedly positive serology (IHA >1280), and surgical identification of parasitic cuticular membranes. Cystic peritoneal malignancy/carcinomatosis was refuted by normal hematologic parameters and direct microscopy demonstrating parasitic hooks and scoleces.
case_prompt:
A 21-year-old man residing in a rural area in northern Morocco presents to the hospital with progressive right hypochondriac pain associated with nausea and vomiting. He reports an indolent history of mild, intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort dating back twelve years, which has acutely intensified over recent weeks. He reports regular daily contact with a domestic dog over the past year. He denies cough, dyspnea, jaundice, melena, or fever.

On physical examination, the patient is clinically stable, afebrile, and in moderate discomfort from abdominal pain. Abdominal examination demonstrates tenderness localized to the right hypochondrium without rigidity or rebound tenderness. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal.

Baseline laboratory testing reveals a normal complete blood count without leukocytosis or peripheral eosinophilia. Liver function tests, including serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT), are completely normal. A plain chest radiograph is normal.

Abdominal imaging (ultrasound and computed tomography) reveals multiple cystic lesions involving the liver and the peritoneal cavity. Within the liver, four cysts are identified in segments VI and VII (three unilocular and one multilocular, measuring 105 x 90 mm, 83 x 31 mm, 43 x 28 mm, and 30 x 19 mm). In the peritoneal cavity, multiple unilocular cystic collections are identified, including five cysts in the left iliac fossa (measuring approximately 30 x 24 mm) and one cyst in the right iliac flank (measuring 25 x 38 mm). Morphologically, the hepatic and peritoneal cysts demonstrate unilocular fluid collections, daughter vesicles, and mixed solid-cystic components.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Congenital Polycystic Disease and Benign Mesenteric Cysts
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the extensive multifocal intrahepatic and extrahepatic peritoneal cystic involvement in a young adult, but disproven by characteristic hydatid cyst morphology (types CE1, CE2, and CE3a / Gharbi IV), strongly positive serology (>1280), and microscopic identification of parasitic hooks.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Abdominal radiography [ultrasound (US) and computed tomography (CT)] revealed multiple hydatid cysts in the liver... and peritoneum... The cysts were classified as type IV according to the Gharbi classification, and type CE1, CE2 and CE3a according to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification... Hydatid serology performed in a private laboratory in Laarach, using the indirect haemagglutination technique (IHA), was positive [the titre >1280 (the positivity threshold is >=320)].

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to widespread multilocular peritoneal seeding involving the iliac fossae, mesentery, and liver, but refuted by normal baseline laboratory parameters, absence of constitutional cachexia, and confirmation of non-viable parasitic scoleces and cuticles upon surgical exploration.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Laboratory parameters, liver function tests [aspartate transaminase (AST) and alanine transaminase (ALT)] and complete blood count showed no abnormalities (the eosinophil level was normal)... Intra-operatively, multiple cysts of varying sizes were discovered, involving almost the entire right hepatic lobe, along with the gall bladder intact, the greater omentum, the mesentery, the small intestine, the pelvis

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: High-titer hydatid serology (IHA >1280, Novalisa IgG 30.30 NTU) followed by median laparotomy revealing extensive cyst dissemination and microscopic demonstration of Echinococcus granulosus cuticular hooks and invaginated/devaginated scoleces confirmed disseminated hydatid disease.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Hydatid serology performed in our laboratory indicated a titre of 30.30 NTU [Novalisa Echinoccus IgG, ELISA (the positivity threshold is 11 NTU)]... Upon microscopic examination of the contents obtained by scraping the internal face of each cuticle, hooks of E. granulosus were identified at the pelvic part. Additionally, hooks, invaginated and devaginated scolex of this parasite were observed in the peritoneal and hepatic parts.

editor_comments: Strict admission breakpoint preserved at the baseline laboratory and abdominal ultrasound/CT imaging stage, prior to send-out serologies, albendazole therapy, and laparotomy. Zero pathogen names or spoilers in the presentation.
